import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks whether a finite representation of a knot can be recognized as
representing the unknot in deterministic polynomial time.

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
-/

open Computability Turing

namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- A point in three-dimensional real space. -/
abbrev Point := Fin 3 → ℝ

/-- Parses a self-delimiting bit string into binary words. A data bit is prefixed by `true`,
while `false` separates consecutive words. -/
def decodeBinaryWordsAux : List Bool → List Bool → Option (List (List Bool))
  | [], word => some [word.reverse]
  | false :: code, word =>
      (decodeBinaryWordsAux code []).map fun words => word.reverse :: words
  | true :: bit :: code, word => decodeBinaryWordsAux code (bit :: word)
  | [true], _ => none

/-- Parses a bit string as a list of binary natural numbers. -/
def decodeNumbers (code : List Bool) : Option (List ℕ) :=
  (decodeBinaryWordsAux code []).map fun words => words.map Computability.decodeNat

/-- Groups a list of natural numbers into points in three-dimensional real space. -/
def numbersToVertices : List ℕ → Option (List Point)
  | [] => some []
  | x :: y :: z :: ns =>
      (numbersToVertices ns).map fun vertices => ![(x : ℝ), (y : ℝ), (z : ℝ)] :: vertices
  | _ => none

/-- Decodes a bit string as the vertices of a closed polygonal curve in real three-space. -/
def decodePolygon (code : List Bool) : Option (List Point) :=
  (decodeNumbers code).bind numbersToVertices

/-- The geometric image of the closed polygonal curve through the listed vertices, in order. -/
def polygonImage (vertices : List Point) : Set Point :=
  {p | ∃ i : ℕ, i + 1 < vertices.length ∧
      p ∈ segment ℝ (vertices.getD i 0) (vertices.getD (i + 1) 0)} ∪
    segment ℝ (vertices.getD (vertices.length - 1) 0) (vertices.getD 0 0)

/-- A fixed triangular polygonal representative of the unknot. -/
def standardUnknot : Set Point :=
  polygonImage [![0, 0, 0], ![1, 0, 0], ![0, 1, 0]]

/-- A polygon represents the unknot when an ambient homeomorphism of real three-space carries its
geometric image to the fixed triangular unknot. -/
def RepresentsUnknot (vertices : List Point) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : Point ≃ₜ Point, h '' polygonImage vertices = standardUnknot

/-- The decision problem on bit strings which accepts exactly encodings of polygonal unknots.
Malformed encodings and encodings not representing the unknot are rejected. -/
noncomputable def unknotLanguage (code : List Bool) : Bool :=
  match decodePolygon code with
  | none => false
  | some vertices => @ite Bool (RepresentsUnknot vertices) (Classical.propDecidable _) true false

/--
**Unknotting problem.** Can unknots, given by a finite polygonal-knot representation, be
recognized by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the representation size?

Here bit strings encode closed polygonal curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and `unknotLanguage` accepts
exactly those whose geometric image is ambiently homeomorphic to a fixed triangular unknot. The
right-hand side says precisely that this decision problem belongs to the complexity class P.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem : answer(sorry) ↔
    Nonempty (TM2ComputableInPolyTime finEncodingListBool finEncodingBoolBool unknotLanguage) := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem
modeling_decisions: Used a concrete finite PL-knot representation: bit strings encode ordered vertices of a closed polygonal curve in ℝ³ with nonnegative integer coordinates. Every tame knot has such a lattice-polygon representative after scaling and translation.

Used a self-delimiting binary serialization: each coordinate bit is prefixed by `true`, and `false` separates coordinates. Thus serialization has constant-factor overhead relative to the coordinate bit lengths, and the Mathlib Turing-machine bound is measured in the actual input length.

Defined unknottedness by existence of an ambient homeomorphism of ℝ³ carrying the polygonal image to a fixed triangular circle. For polygonal (tame) knots this is the standard unknot condition; using homeomorphism rather than ambient isotopy does not change whether a knot is the unknot.
The language returns false on malformed codes and on polygonal images that are not ambiently homeomorphic to the standard unknot, including degenerate and self-intersecting images.

Expressed class-P membership directly as nonemptiness of Mathlib's `TM2ComputableInPolyTime` structure using the repository's identity encoding of `List Bool` and Mathlib's Boolean output encoding. A positive `answer(sorry)` therefore means that unknot recognition is in P.

import FormalConjecturesUtil
import FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP

/-!
# The unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks whether unknots can be recognized in polynomial time: given a
finite description of a knot, decide in time polynomial in the size of the description whether
the knot is the trivial knot. In other words, is the unknotting problem in the complexity
class `P`?

The problem is known to be in `NP` (Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger) and in `co-NP` (Lackenby;
Kuperberg assuming GRH). Membership in `P` is open; Lackenby has announced a quasi-polynomial
time algorithm.

We follow Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger and represent a knot by a *polygonal representation*:
the list of the vertices of a closed polygon in `ℝ³`, in cyclic order, with integer
coordinates written in binary. They show that this representation is polynomial-time equivalent
to knot diagrams (with the crossing number as size). Since `P` is closed under complement, it
does not matter whether one asks to recognize unknottedness or knottedness.

A polygon is the unknot when some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps it onto the standard round
circle. An input that does not describe a simple closed curve is never an unknot. The
decision problem is formalised as a language over `{0, 1}`: a bit string is in the language when
it is the code of a polygon that is the unknot. This language is in `P` if and only if the
unknot can be recognized in polynomial time.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Unknotting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- J. Hass, J. C. Lagarias, N. Pippenger, *The computational complexity of knot and link
  problems*, J. ACM 46 (1999), 185–211. [arXiv:math/9807016](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807016)
- M. Lackenby, *The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm*, Adv. Math. 387
  (2021). [arXiv:1604.00290](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00290)
-/

open Computability ComplexityTheory

namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- The point of `ℝ³` with integer coordinates `v 0, v 1, v 2`. -/
def toPoint (v : Fin 3 → ℤ) : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 fun i => (v i : ℝ)

/-- The closed polygon in `ℝ³` with vertices `v₀, v₁, …, vₙ₋₁` (in this cyclic order): the union
of the straight segments `[vᵢ, vᵢ₊₁]`, indices taken modulo `n`. -/
def polygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)) :=
  ⋃ e ∈ v.zip (v.rotate 1), segment ℝ (toPoint e.1) (toPoint e.2)

/-- The standard unknot: the unit circle in the coordinate plane `x₂ = 0` of `ℝ³`. -/
def standardCircle : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)) :=
  {x | ‖x‖ = 1 ∧ x 2 = 0}

/-- A subset `K ⊆ ℝ³` is an unknot (a trivial knot) if some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps `K` onto
the standard circle. In particular `K` is then a simple closed curve. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3))) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) ≃ₜ EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3), h '' K = standardCircle

/-- The binary code of an integer: a sign bit followed by the binary digits of its absolute
value. -/
def encodeInt (z : ℤ) : List Bool :=
  decide (z < 0) :: encodeNat z.natAbs

/-- Decoding of `encodeInt`. -/
def decodeInt : List Bool → ℤ
  | [] => 0
  | s :: l => if s then -(decodeNat l : ℤ) else decodeNat l

lemma decodeInt_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : decodeInt (encodeInt z) = z := by
  simp only [encodeInt, decodeInt, decode_encodeNat]
  split_ifs with h <;> simp only [decide_eq_true_eq] at h <;> omega

/-- Groups a list of integers into consecutive triples. Fails if the length is not a multiple
of three. -/
def groupTriples : List ℤ → Option (List (Fin 3 → ℤ))
  | [] => some []
  | a :: b :: c :: l => (groupTriples l).map (![a, b, c] :: ·)
  | _ => none

lemma groupTriples_flatMap_ofFn (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :
    groupTriples (v.flatMap List.ofFn) = some v := by
  induction v with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons p v ih =>
    have hp : ![p 0, p 1, p 2] = p := by
      funext i
      fin_cases i <;> rfl
    simp [List.ofFn_succ, groupTriples, ih, hp]

/-- The code of a polygon over the alphabet `Option Bool`: each coordinate, in order, is written
as the separator `none` followed by its binary code. -/
def encodePolygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : List (Option Bool) :=
  ((v.flatMap List.ofFn).map fun z => (encodeInt z).map some).flatMap (none :: ·)

/-- Decoding of `encodePolygon`. -/
def decodePolygon (w : List (Option Bool)) : Option (List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :=
  match w.splitOnP Option.isNone with
  | [] :: chunks => groupTriples (chunks.map fun c => decodeInt (c.map (·.getD false)))
  | _ => none

lemma splitOnP_isNone_append_flatMap_cons (cs : List (List (Option Bool)))
    (h : ∀ c ∈ cs, none ∉ c) (c : List (Option Bool)) (hc : none ∉ c) :
    (c ++ cs.flatMap (none :: ·)).splitOnP Option.isNone = c :: cs := by
  induction cs generalizing c with
  | nil =>
    rw [List.flatMap_nil, List.append_nil]
    exact List.splitOnP_eq_single _ _ fun x hx hx' =>
      hc (Option.isNone_iff_eq_none.mp hx' ▸ hx)
  | cons c' cs ih =>
    rw [List.flatMap_cons, List.cons_append,
      List.splitOnP_first _ _ (fun x hx hx' => hc (Option.isNone_iff_eq_none.mp hx' ▸ hx))
        none rfl,
      ih (fun d hd => h d (List.mem_cons_of_mem _ hd)) c' (h c' List.mem_cons_self)]

lemma decodePolygon_encodePolygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :
    decodePolygon (encodePolygon v) = some v := by
  rw [decodePolygon, encodePolygon, ← List.nil_append (List.flatMap _ _),
    splitOnP_isNone_append_flatMap_cons _ (fun c hc => by
      obtain ⟨z, -, rfl⟩ := List.mem_map.mp hc
      simp) [] (by simp)]
  simp [Function.comp_def, decodeInt_encodeInt, groupTriples_flatMap_ofFn]

/-- The two-bit code of a symbol of the alphabet `Option Bool`. -/
def encodeSymbol : Option Bool → List Bool
  | some b => [true, b]
  | none => [false, false]

/-- Decoding of a string of two-bit symbol codes. -/
def decodeSymbols : List Bool → Option (List (Option Bool))
  | [] => some []
  | true :: b :: l => (decodeSymbols l).map (some b :: ·)
  | false :: _ :: l => (decodeSymbols l).map (none :: ·)
  | [_] => none

lemma decodeSymbols_flatMap_encodeSymbol (w : List (Option Bool)) :
    decodeSymbols (w.flatMap encodeSymbol) = some w := by
  induction w with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons s w ih => cases s <;> simp [encodeSymbol, decodeSymbols, ih]

/-- The binary encoding of polygons with integer vertices. -/
def polygonEncoding : FinEncoding (List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) where
  Γ := Bool
  encode v := (encodePolygon v).flatMap encodeSymbol
  decode w := (decodeSymbols w).bind decodePolygon
  decode_encode v := by
    simp [decodeSymbols_flatMap_encodeSymbol, decodePolygon_encodePolygon]
  ΓFin := Bool.fintype

/-- The code of the one-vertex polygon `(1, -1, 0)`: the three coordinates are written as
`none, some false, some true`, `none, some true, some true`, `none, some false`, then each
symbol as two bits. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem polygonEncoding_encode_example :
    polygonEncoding.encode [![1, -1, 0]] =
      [false, false, true, false, true, true, false, false, true, true, true, true, false, false,
        true, false] := by
  simp [polygonEncoding, encodePolygon, encodeInt, encodeNat, encodeNum, encodePosNum, encodeSymbol,
    List.ofFn_succ]

/-- The empty list of vertices describes the empty set. -/
@[category test, AMS 57]
theorem polygon_nil : polygon [] = ∅ := by
  simp [polygon]

/-- The empty set is not a knot, so it is not the unknot. -/
@[category test, AMS 57]
theorem not_isUnknot_empty : ¬ IsUnknot ∅ := by
  rintro ⟨h, hh⟩
  have : EuclideanSpace.single (0 : Fin 3) (1 : ℝ) ∈ standardCircle := by
    simp [standardCircle]
  rw [← hh] at this
  simp at this

open scoped Classical in
/-- Unknot recognition as a language over `{0, 1}`: a bit string is accepted exactly when it is
the code of a polygon (with integer vertices) that is the unknot. -/
noncomputable def unknotRecognition : DecisionProblem := fun w =>
  decide (∃ v, polygonEncoding.decode w = some v ∧ IsUnknot (polygon v))

/-- The empty bit string is the code of the empty polygon, which is not a knot. -/
@[category test, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotRecognition_nil : unknotRecognition [] = false := by
  have : polygonEncoding.decode [] = some [] := rfl
  simp [unknotRecognition, this, polygon_nil, not_isUnknot_empty]

/--
**The unknotting problem.** Can unknots be recognized in polynomial time? That is, is the
unknotting problem — given a knot, described as a closed polygon in `ℝ³` with integer vertices
written in binary, decide whether it is the unknot — in the complexity class `P`?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem : answer(sorry) ↔ unknotRecognition ∈ P := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem

modeling_decisions: Knot representation: following Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger (the primary source cited by the article), a knot is given by the list of vertices (in cyclic order, type `List (Fin 3 → ℤ)`) of a closed polygon in ℝ³ with integer coordinates; HLP state this representation is polynomial-time equivalent to knot diagrams with crossing number as size, and the decomposition notes allow any standard representation. `polygon v` is the union of segments between cyclically consecutive vertices (`v.zip (v.rotate 1)`).

Input size: coordinates are written in binary (sign bit + binary digits, Mathlib's `encodeNat`), separated by a separator symbol, then the 4-letter alphabet `Option Bool` is block-coded into 2 bits, so the code length is linear in the number of bits needed to write the vertices — HLP's 'input length'. The `FinEncoding` field `decode_encode` is proved, so every polygon has a code. Decoding is lenient (e.g. leading zeros accepted), which does not affect P-membership since decoding is polynomial-time.

Unknot: `IsUnknot K := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle` (standard round unit circle in the plane x₂ = 0). This is the textbook definition of knot equivalence via an ambient homeomorphism; orientation-preservation is not required because the standard circle is invariant under the reflection x₂ ↦ −x₂, and for polygonal (tame) knots this coincides with PL ambient isotopy as used by HLP. Homeomorphisms of ℝ³ rather than S³ are used (equivalent for tame knots).

Language vs promise problem: inputs that are not simple closed curves (or are not valid codes) are rejected, mirroring HLP's formulation 'Is D a knot diagram that represents the trivial knot?'. Since simplicity of an integer polygon is checkable in polynomial time, P-membership of this language is equivalent to polynomial-time unknot recognition on genuine knots.

Complexity class: the statement uses the repository's existing `ComplexityTheory.P` (imported from `FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP`, an idiom already used by several Wikipedia files importing other problem files), whose model is Mathlib's TM2 stack machine with polynomial step bound in the input length. Since P is closed under complement, asking for unknottedness rather than knottedness is immaterial.
The decision function `unknotRecognition` is defined with classical `decide` (noncomputable), as in the repo's treatment of languages as arbitrary `List Bool → Bool`.

/-!

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
-/

open Computability Turing

namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- A step of the cubic lattice: a coordinate axis and a choice of positive or negative
direction. -/
abbrev LatticeStep := Fin 3 × Bool

/-- Decode three-bit blocks `000`, ..., `101` as the six directed coordinate steps.
The other blocks, and a final block of fewer than three bits, are invalid. -/
def decodeSteps : List Bool → Option (List LatticeStep)
  | [] => some []
  | false :: false :: false :: bs => (⟨0, false⟩ :: ·) <$> decodeSteps bs
  | false :: false :: true :: bs => (⟨0, true⟩ :: ·) <$> decodeSteps bs
  | false :: true :: false :: bs => (⟨1, false⟩ :: ·) <$> decodeSteps bs
  | false :: true :: true :: bs => (⟨1, true⟩ :: ·) <$> decodeSteps bs
  | true :: false :: false :: bs => (⟨2, false⟩ :: ·) <$> decodeSteps bs
  | true :: false :: true :: bs => (⟨2, true⟩ :: ·) <$> decodeSteps bs
  | _ => none

/-- The displacement in `ℤ³` represented by one lattice step. -/
def displacement (s : LatticeStep) : Fin 3 → ℤ :=
  fun i => if i = s.1 then if s.2 then -1 else 1 else 0

/-- Successive vertices of the lattice walk, including its initial vertex. -/
def vertices : List LatticeStep → List (Fin 3 → ℤ)
  | [] => [0]
  | s :: ss => 0 :: (vertices ss).map (displacement s + ·)

/-- A bit string is a cubic-lattice knot code when it describes a closed self-avoiding polygon.
The lower bound excludes degenerate polygons. -/

unknot in deterministic polynomial time. We use cubic-lattice polygons, encoded with three bits
per directed edge, as a standard finite representation of piecewise-linear knots.

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)

open Computability Turing

namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- The six directed unit steps in the cubic lattice. -/
inductive LatticeDirection
  | posX | negX | posY | negY | posZ | negZ
  deriving DecidableEq

/-- The integer displacement represented by a cubic-lattice direction. -/
def LatticeDirection.step : LatticeDirection → ℤ × ℤ × ℤ
  | .posX => (1, 0, 0)
  | .negX => (-1, 0, 0)
  | .posY => (0, 1, 0)
  | .negY => (0, -1, 0)
  | .posZ => (0, 0, 1)
  | .negZ => (0, 0, -1)

/-- Decode a three-bit block as one of the six cubic-lattice directions. -/
def decodeDirection : Bool → Bool → Bool → Option LatticeDirection
  | false, false, false => some .posX
  | false, false, true => some .negX
  | false, true, false => some .posY
  | false, true, true => some .negY
  | true, false, false => some .posZ
  | true, false, true => some .negZ
  | true, true, _ => none

/-- Decode a bitstring in three-bit blocks as a cubic-lattice walk. -/
def decodeWalk : List Bool → Option (List LatticeDirection)
  | [] => some []
  | a :: b :: c :: rest => do
      let d ← decodeDirection a b c
      let ds ← decodeWalk rest
      pure (d :: ds)
  | _ => none

/-- The successive vertices of a cubic-lattice walk, starting at the origin. -/
def latticeVertices (ds : List LatticeDirection) : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) :=
  ds.map LatticeDirection.step |>.scanl (· + ·) 0

/-- A walk is a cubic-lattice polygon when it is a closed self-avoiding walk with at least four
edges. -/
def IsLatticePolygon (ds : List LatticeDirection) : Prop :=
  4 ≤ ds.length ∧ (latticeVertices ds).getLast? = some 0 ∧
    (latticeVertices ds).dropLast.Pairwise (· ≠ ·)

/-- Regard an integer lattice point as a point of Euclidean three-space. -/
def latticePointToReal (p : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) : ℝ × ℝ × ℝ :=
  (p.1, p.2.1, p.2.2)

/-- The polygonal trace of a cubic-lattice walk starting at `p`. -/
def latticeTraceFrom : (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) → List LatticeDirection → Set (ℝ × ℝ × ℝ)
  | _, [] => ∅
  | p, d :: ds =>
      segment ℝ (latticePointToReal p) (latticePointToReal (p + d.step)) ∪
        latticeTraceFrom (p + d.step) ds

/-- The polygonal trace of a cubic-lattice walk starting at the origin. -/
def latticeTrace (ds : List LatticeDirection) : Set (ℝ × ℝ × ℝ) :=
  latticeTraceFrom 0 ds

/-- A fixed square polygon representing the unknot. -/
def standardUnknot : List LatticeDirection :=
  [.posX, .posY, .negX, .negY]

/-- A cubic-lattice polygon is unknotted when an ambient homeomorphism of three-space carries its
trace to the fixed square unknot. -/
def IsUnknot (ds : List LatticeDirection) : Prop :=
  IsLatticePolygon ds ∧ ∃ h : (ℝ × ℝ × ℝ) ≃ₜ (ℝ × ℝ × ℝ),
    h '' latticeTrace ds = latticeTrace standardUnknot

open scoped Classical in
/-- The Boolean language of encodings of unknotted cubic-lattice polygons. Invalid encodings are
rejected. -/
noncomputable def unknotLanguage : List Bool → Bool := fun input =>
  match decodeWalk input with
  | none => false
  | some ds => if IsUnknot ds then true else false

/--
Can unknots be recognized in polynomial time? More precisely, is the language of finite
three-bit encodings of unknotted cubic-lattice polygons decidable by a deterministic Turing
machine in time polynomial in the input length?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ Nonempty
      (TM2ComputableInPolyTime finEncodingListBool finEncodingBoolBool unknotLanguage) := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks for an algorithm that decides, given a finite description of a knot
(for example a knot diagram or a closed polygon in $\mathbb{R}^3$), whether the knot is the
unknot. Haken (1961) showed that the problem is decidable, Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger (1999)
showed that it is in NP, and Lackenby (2016) showed that it is in co-NP. It is open whether the
problem is in P, i.e. whether unknots can be recognized in polynomial time. In 2021 Lackenby
announced a quasi-polynomial time algorithm; this does not settle the question.

We represent a knot as a closed polygon in $\mathbb{R}^3$, given by the list of its vertices,
which have integer coordinates. The input size is the number of symbols in the binary encoding
of the coordinates. Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger (Section 1 and Section 7) show that this
representation is polynomial-time equivalent to knot diagrams, with the input length
polynomially related to the number of crossings. For polynomial time we use the Turing machine
model `Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime` of Mathlib, as in `FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP`.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Unknotting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [J. Hass, J. C. Lagarias, N. Pippenger, *The computational complexity of knot and link
  problems*, J. ACM 46 (1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807016)
- [M. Lackenby, *The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm*,
  Adv. Math. 387 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00290)
-/

open Computability

namespace UnknottingProblem

local notation "ℝ³" => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/- ### Knots and the unknot -/

/-- The point of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the given integer coordinates. -/
def toPoint (p : ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) : ℝ³ := !₂[(p.1 : ℝ), (p.2.1 : ℝ), (p.2.2 : ℝ)]

/-- The closed polygon in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the vertices `v` (listed in cyclic order): the union
of the closed segments from each vertex to the next one, and from the last vertex back to the
first one. -/
def polygon (v : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : Set ℝ³ :=
  ⋃ e ∈ v.zip (v.rotate 1), segment ℝ (toPoint e.1) (toPoint e.2)

/-- A subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a knot if it is homeomorphic to the circle $S^1$.
For a closed polygon this says that the polygon is simple (it does not intersect itself). -/
def IsKnot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := Nonempty (K ≃ₜ Circle)

/-- The standard unknot: the unit circle in the $xy$-plane of $\mathbb{R}^3$. -/
def standardUnknot : Set ℝ³ := {x | x 0 ^ 2 + x 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ x 2 = 0}

/-- A subset $K$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is an unknot (a trivial knot) if it is equivalent to the standard
unknot, i.e. some homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^3$ maps $K$ onto the standard unknot.

The standard unknot is preserved by the reflection $(x, y, z) \mapsto (x, y, -z)$, so this is
the same as requiring an orientation preserving homeomorphism, or an ambient isotopy. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardUnknot

/-- The polygon with no vertices is empty. -/
@[category API, AMS 57]
theorem polygon_nil : polygon [] = ∅ := by
  simp [polygon]

/-- A triangle is a knot. -/
@[category test, AMS 57]
theorem isKnot_triangle : IsKnot (polygon [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)]) := by
  sorry

/-- A triangle is an unknot. -/
@[category test, AMS 57]
theorem isUnknot_triangle : IsUnknot (polygon [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)]) := by
  sorry

@[category API, AMS 57]
theorem IsUnknot.isKnot {K : Set ℝ³} (hK : IsUnknot K) : IsKnot K := by
  sorry

/- ### Binary encoding of a list of vertices

The input of the algorithm is the list of vertices of a polygon. It is encoded as a word over a
three letter alphabet: each coordinate is written in binary (a sign bit followed by the binary
digits of its absolute value), and consecutive coordinates are separated by a separator symbol.
The length of the encoding of a polygon is therefore proportional to the number of bits needed to
write down its vertices in binary. -/

/-- The alphabet of the encoding: the two binary digits and a separator. -/
inductive Symbol
  | bit (b : Bool)
  | sep
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- The bit carried by a symbol, if any. -/
def Symbol.toBit : Symbol → Option Bool
  | bit b => some b
  | sep => none

/-- Binary encoding of an integer: a sign bit (`true` for nonnegative integers) followed by the
binary digits of its absolute value. -/
def encodeInt (z : ℤ) : List Bool := decide (0 ≤ z) :: encodeNat z.natAbs

/-- Decoding of an integer from a list of bits, the inverse of `encodeInt`. -/
def decodeInt : List Bool → ℤ
  | [] => 0
  | b :: l => if b then (decodeNat l : ℤ) else -(decodeNat l : ℤ)

@[category API, AMS 68]
theorem decodeInt_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : decodeInt (encodeInt z) = z := by
  rcases le_or_gt 0 z with h | h
  · simp [encodeInt, decodeInt, h]
  · simp [encodeInt, decodeInt, h.not_ge, abs_of_neg h]

/-- The list of all coordinates of a list of vertices. -/
def coords (v : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : List ℤ := v.flatMap fun p => [p.1, p.2.1, p.2.2]

/-- Groups a list of coordinates into vertices, the inverse of `coords`. -/
def groupCoords : List ℤ → Option (List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ))
  | [] => some []
  | x :: y :: z :: l => (groupCoords l).map ((x, y, z) :: ·)
  | _ => none

@[category API, AMS 68]
theorem groupCoords_coords (v : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : groupCoords (coords v) = some v := by
  induction v with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons p v ih => simpa [coords, groupCoords] using ih

/-- The encoding of a list of vertices: the binary encodings of the coordinates, separated by
`Symbol.sep`. -/
def encodeVertices (v : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) : List Symbol :=
  [Symbol.sep].intercalate ((coords v).map fun z => (encodeInt z).map Symbol.bit)

/-- The decoding of a list of vertices from a word, the inverse of `encodeVertices`. -/
def decodeVertices (w : List Symbol) : Option (List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) :=
  groupCoords (((w.splitOn Symbol.sep).filter (· ≠ [])).map fun b =>
    decodeInt (b.filterMap Symbol.toBit))

@[category API, AMS 68]
theorem decodeVertices_encodeVertices (v : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) :
    decodeVertices (encodeVertices v) = some v := by
  rcases v with _ | ⟨p, v⟩
  · rfl
  · have h1 : (encodeVertices (p :: v)).splitOn Symbol.sep =
        (coords (p :: v)).map fun z => (encodeInt z).map Symbol.bit :=
      List.splitOn_intercalate ((coords (p :: v)).map fun z => (encodeInt z).map Symbol.bit)
        Symbol.sep (by simp) (by simp [coords])
    rw [decodeVertices, h1, List.filter_eq_self.2 (by simp [encodeInt])]
    simp [Function.comp_def, Symbol.toBit, decodeInt_encodeInt, groupCoords_coords]

/-- The binary encoding of lists of vertices, as a `Computability.FinEncoding`. -/
def vertexListEncoding : FinEncoding (List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ)) where
  Γ := Symbol
  encode := encodeVertices
  decode := decodeVertices
  decode_encode := decodeVertices_encodeVertices
  ΓFin := inferInstance

/- ### The unknotting problem -/

/--
**Unknotting problem**: can unknots be recognized in polynomial time?

That is, is there an algorithm which, given the list of vertices of a closed polygon in
$\mathbb{R}^3$ that is a knot, decides whether the knot is the unknot, and whose running time is
bounded by a polynomial in the length of the binary encoding of the vertices?

Formally: is there a function `f` from lists of vertices to `Bool` that is computable in
polynomial time (with respect to `vertexListEncoding`) by a deterministic Turing machine, such
that for every list of vertices `v` whose polygon is a knot, `f v = true` if and only if this
knot is the unknot?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ f : List (ℤ × ℤ × ℤ) → Bool,
      ComplexityTheory.IsComputableInPolyTime vertexListEncoding finEncodingBoolBool f ∧
      ∀ v, IsKnot (polygon v) → (f v = true ↔ IsUnknot (polygon v)) := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks whether the unknot can be recognized in polynomial time. We use closed
braid words as finite representations of links. By Markov's theorem, two closed braids represent
the same link exactly when their braid words are related by braid relations, conjugations, and
stabilizations.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Unknotting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, Markov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_theorem)
-/

namespace UnknottingProblem

open Computability Turing

/-- A braid code consists of a number of strands and a word of signed, zero-based generators.
The Boolean sign `true` denotes the positive generator. -/
abbrev BraidCode := ℕ × List (ℕ × Bool)

/-- A braid code is valid when it has at least one strand and every generator `i` satisfies
`i + 1 < n`, where `n` is the number of strands. -/
def IsValid (b : BraidCode) : Prop :=
  0 < b.1 ∧ ∀ g ∈ b.2, g.1 + 1 < b.1

/-- One application, in an arbitrary word context, of a defining relation for the braid group.
The constructors give inverse cancellation, far commutation, and the Artin braid relation. -/
inductive BraidStep : BraidCode → BraidCode → Prop
  | cancel (n i : ℕ) (s : Bool) (u v : List (ℕ × Bool)) (hi : i + 1 < n)
      (h : IsValid (n, u ++ v)) :
      BraidStep (n, u ++ (i, s) :: (i, !s) :: v) (n, u ++ v)
  | commute (n i j : ℕ) (s t : Bool) (u v : List (ℕ × Bool)) (hij : i + 1 < j)
      (h : IsValid (n, u ++ (i, s) :: (j, t) :: v)) :
      BraidStep (n, u ++ (i, s) :: (j, t) :: v) (n, u ++ (j, t) :: (i, s) :: v)
  | braid (n i : ℕ) (u v : List (ℕ × Bool)) (hi : i + 2 < n)
      (h : IsValid (n, u ++ (i, true) :: (i + 1, true) :: (i, true) :: v)) :
      BraidStep (n, u ++ (i, true) :: (i + 1, true) :: (i, true) :: v)
        (n, u ++ (i + 1, true) :: (i, true) :: (i + 1, true) :: v)

/-- One Markov move on braid words: a braid relation, conjugation by a generator, or stabilization
by one positive or negative crossing. -/
inductive MarkovStep : BraidCode → BraidCode → Prop
  | braid {a b : BraidCode} (h : BraidStep a b) : MarkovStep a b
  | conjugate (n i : ℕ) (s : Bool) (w : List (ℕ × Bool)) (hi : i + 1 < n)
      (h : IsValid (n, w)) :
      MarkovStep (n, w) (n, (i, s) :: w ++ [(i, !s)])
  | stabilize (n : ℕ) (s : Bool) (w : List (ℕ × Bool)) (h : IsValid (n, w)) :
      MarkovStep (n, w) (n + 1, w ++ [(n - 1, s)])

/-- Markov equivalence is the equivalence relation generated by Markov moves. -/
def MarkovEquivalent : BraidCode → BraidCode → Prop :=
  Relation.EqvGen MarkovStep

/-- Run lengths of `true` bits separated by `false` bits. -/
def decodeRuns : List Bool → List ℕ
  | [] => [0]
  | true :: bits =>
      match decodeRuns bits with
      | n :: ns => (n + 1) :: ns
      | [] => []
  | false :: bits => 0 :: decodeRuns bits

/-- Decode a bit string as a braid. The first run gives one less than the strand count. Each later
run `k` gives generator `k / 2`, with sign determined by the parity of `k`. -/
def decodeBraid (bits : List Bool) : BraidCode :=
  match decodeRuns bits with
  | [] => (1, [])
  | n :: ks => (n + 1, ks.map fun k => (k / 2, k % 2 = 1))

/-- A code represents the unknot when it is valid and Markov equivalent to the trivial one-strand
braid. -/
def IsUnknotCode (b : BraidCode) : Prop :=
  IsValid b ∧ MarkovEquivalent b (1, [])

open scoped Classical in
/-- The Boolean language of bit strings that decode to closed braid representatives of the unknot.
Invalid braid codes are rejected. -/
noncomputable def unknotLanguage (bits : List Bool) : Bool :=
  if IsUnknotCode (decodeBraid bits) then true else false

/--
**Unknotting problem.** Can unknots, given by finite closed-braid representations, be recognized by
a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the representation's bit length?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem :
    answer(sorry) ↔ Nonempty (TM2ComputableInPolyTime finEncodingListBool finEncodingBoolBool
      unknotLanguage) := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem
modeling_decisions: Used finite closed-braid words as the standard finite representation of knots. By Markov's theorem, a valid closed braid represents the unknot exactly when it is Markov equivalent to the trivial one-strand braid.

Represented braid-group equality by the equivalence closure of contextual inverse cancellation, far commutation, and the Artin braid relation; represented Markov equivalence by additionally closing under generator conjugation and positive or negative stabilization.

Used a total unary run-length encoding from `List Bool` to braid codes. The number of strands and generator indices therefore contribute explicitly to bit length; this is polynomially related to standard finite braid/diagram encodings rather than hiding unbounded data in one alphabet symbol.

Defined the decision language to accept exactly valid codes Markov equivalent to the trivial one-strand braid. Invalid codes and valid braids whose closures are nontrivial knots or links are rejected.

Expressed deterministic polynomial time using Mathlib's `Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime`, with the repository's Boolean-list input and Boolean output encodings. Wrapped existence of such a machine in `Nonempty` to state a proposition.
Used `answer(sorry) ↔ ...` because the source asks a yes/no question; substituting `True` records the positive answer that unknot recognition lies in P.

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks for an algorithm that recognizes the unknot, given a finite
representation of a knot. It is decidable (Haken, 1961), it lies in `NP` (Hass, Lagarias and
Pippenger, 1999) and in `co-NP` (Lackenby, 2016). Whether it lies in `P`, that is, whether
unknots can be recognized in polynomial time, is open.

Following Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, a knot is a simple closed polygon in `ℝ³`, represented by
the cyclic list of its vertices, which have integer coordinates. The input length is the number of
bits needed to write these coordinates in binary. This representation is polynomial-time
equivalent to knot diagrams (with the crossing number as size), so the choice of representation
does not affect the question. As in Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, the decision problem is
formulated as a language: an input is accepted if and only if it is a knot and this knot is
trivial.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Unknotting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- J. Hass, J. C. Lagarias, N. Pippenger, *The computational complexity of knot and link problems*,
  J. ACM 46 (1999), 185–211. [arXiv:math/9807016](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807016)
- M. Lackenby, *The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm*,
  Adv. Math. 387 (2021). [arXiv:1604.00290](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00290)
-/

open Computability

namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- Euclidean three-space. -/
local notation "ℝ³" => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/- ### Polygonal knots -/

/-- The point of `ℝ³` with integer coordinates `p 0`, `p 1`, `p 2`. -/
def toPoint (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) : ℝ³ := WithLp.toLp 2 fun i => (p i : ℝ)

/-- The piecewise-linear parametrisation of the closed polygon with vertex list `v`.
The parameter `(k, t)` is sent to the point at fraction `t` along the `k`-th edge, which joins the
vertex `v[k]` to the cyclically next vertex `v[finRotate v.length k]` (`finRotate` is the cyclic
shift `k ↦ k + 1` of `Fin v.length`, so the last edge joins the last vertex to the first). -/
noncomputable def loop (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) (x : Fin v.length × ℝ) : ℝ³ :=
  (1 - x.2) • toPoint v[x.1] + x.2 • toPoint v[finRotate v.length x.1]

/-- The closed polygon with vertex list `v`, as a subset of `ℝ³`: the union of the segments
joining cyclically consecutive vertices (see `polygon_eq_iUnion_segment`). -/
noncomputable def polygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Set ℝ³ :=
  loop v '' (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Icc 0 1)

/-- The vertex list `v` is a *polygonal knot*: it has at least three vertices and the closed
polygon through them is simple, i.e. its parametrisation `loop v` is injective on one period
`Fin v.length × [0, 1)`. -/
def IsPolygonalKnot (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Prop :=
  3 ≤ v.length ∧ Set.InjOn (loop v) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Ico 0 1)

/-- The standard unknot: the unit circle in the `xy`-plane. -/
def standardCircle : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 2 = 0}

/-- A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an *unknot* (a trivial knot) if some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps it
onto the standard circle. For polygonal knots this is equivalent (by Dehn's lemma) to the
piecewise-linear notion used by Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger: the knot can be deformed, through
simple polygons, to a planar polygon. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle

open scoped Classical in
/-- Unknot recognition as a Boolean function on vertex lists: `isUnknottedPolygon v = true` if and
only if `v` is a polygonal knot and this knot is trivial. Vertex lists that do not describe a knot
are rejected. -/
noncomputable def isUnknottedPolygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Bool :=
  decide (IsPolygonalKnot v ∧ IsUnknot (polygon v))

@[category API, AMS 57]
lemma polygon_eq_iUnion_segment (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :

  ext p

  rw [← hh] at this
  simp at this

  simp [isUnknottedPolygon, IsPolygonalKnot]

/- ### Encoding of polygonal representations

A vertex list is written as a word over a four-letter alphabet: the three coordinates of a vertex
are written in binary and separated by commas, and consecutive vertices are separated by
semicolons. Each letter is then written as two bits. The length of the resulting bit string is,
up to a constant factor, the number of bits of the coordinates: the input length of Hass, Lagarias
and Pippenger. -/

/-- The input alphabet: binary digits, a separator between the coordinates of a vertex and a
separator between consecutive vertices. -/
inductive Alphabet
  | digit (b : Bool)
  | comma
  | semicolon
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- Each letter is written as two bits. -/
def Alphabet.toBits : Alphabet → List Bool
  | digit b => [false, b]
  | comma => [true, false]
  | semicolon => [true, true]

/-- Inverse of `List.flatMap Alphabet.toBits`. -/
def Alphabet.ofBits : List Bool → Option (List Alphabet)
  | [] => some []
  | [_] => none
  | false :: b :: s => (digit b :: ·) <$> ofBits s
  | true :: false :: s => (comma :: ·) <$> ofBits s
  | true :: true :: s => (semicolon :: ·) <$> ofBits s

/-- The binary expansion (least significant digit first) of the natural number
`Encodable.encode z`, where `Encodable.encode : ℤ → ℕ` is the bijection `n ↦ 2n`,
`-(n + 1) ↦ 2n + 1`. -/
def encodeInt (z : ℤ) : List Alphabet :=
  (Nat.digits 2 (Encodable.encode z)).map fun d => .digit (d == 1)

/-- Inverse of `encodeInt`. -/
def decodeInt (l : List Alphabet) : ℤ :=
  Denumerable.ofNat ℤ (Nat.ofDigits 2 (l.map fun s => if s = .digit true then 1 else 0))

/-- The three coordinates of a vertex, separated by commas. -/
def encodeVertex (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) : List Alphabet :=
  [.comma].intercalate ((List.ofFn p).map encodeInt)

/-- Inverse of `encodeVertex`. -/
def decodeVertex (l : List Alphabet) : Option (Fin 3 → ℤ) :=
  match l.splitOn .comma with
  | [a, b, c] => some ![decodeInt a, decodeInt b, decodeInt c]
  | _ => none

/-- The vertices, separated by semicolons. -/
def encodeVertices (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : List Alphabet :=
  [.semicolon].intercalate (v.map encodeVertex)

/-- Inverse of `encodeVertices`. -/
def decodeVertices (l : List Alphabet) : Option (List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :=
  match l.splitOn .semicolon with
  | [[]] => some []
  | parts => parts.mapM decodeVertex

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma Alphabet.ofBits_flatMap_toBits (l : List Alphabet) :
    Alphabet.ofBits (l.flatMap Alphabet.toBits) = some l := by
  induction l with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons a l ih => cases a <;> simp [Alphabet.toBits, Alphabet.ofBits, ih]

lemma decodeInt_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : decodeInt (encodeInt z) = z := by
  have h : ∀ d ∈ Nat.digits 2 (Encodable.encode z),

    intro d hd
    have := Nat.digits_lt_base (by norm_num) hd
    interval_cases d <;> simp
  simp only [decodeInt, encodeInt, List.map_map, Function.comp_def]
  rw [List.map_congr_left h, List.map_id', Nat.ofDigits_digits, Denumerable.ofNat_encode]

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma comma_notMem_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : Alphabet.comma ∉ encodeInt z := by
  simp [encodeInt]

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma semicolon_notMem_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : Alphabet.semicolon ∉ encodeInt z := by
  simp [encodeInt]

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma encodeVertex_eq (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) :
    encodeVertex p = encodeInt (p 0) ++ .comma :: encodeInt (p 1) ++ .comma :: encodeInt (p 2) := by
  simp [encodeVertex, List.intercalate, List.ofFn_succ]

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma decodeVertex_encodeVertex (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) : decodeVertex (encodeVertex p) = some p := by
  have h : (encodeVertex p).splitOn .comma =

    · simp [List.ofFn_succ]
    · simp [comma_notMem_encodeInt]

  rcases v with _ | ⟨p, w⟩
  · rfl
  · have h : (encodeVertices (p :: w)).splitOn .semicolon = (p :: w).map encodeVertex := by
      rw [encodeVertices, List.splitOn_intercalate]
      · simp [semicolon_notMem_encodeVertex]
      · simp
    rw [decodeVertices, h]
    have h2 : ∀ w : List (Fin 3 → ℤ), (w.map encodeVertex).mapM decodeVertex = some w := by
      intro w
      induction w with
      | nil => rfl

    simp [encodeVertex_ne_nil, h2, decodeVertex_encodeVertex]

`Alphabet` (coordinates in binary, separated by commas; vertices separated by semicolons) and each
letter is written as two bits. -/

  Γ := Bool
  encode v := (encodeVertices v).flatMap Alphabet.toBits
  decode s := (Alphabet.ofBits s).bind decodeVertices
  decode_encode v := by simp [Alphabet.ofBits_flatMap_toBits, decodeVertices_encodeVertices]
  ΓFin := inferInstance

lemma polygonEncoding_encode_example :
    polygonEncoding.encode [![0, 0, 0], ![3, -1, 2]] =

    show Encodable.encode (3 : ℤ) = 6 from rfl, show Encodable.encode (-1 : ℤ) = 1 from rfl,

import FormalConjecturesUtil
import FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem is the problem of algorithmically recognizing the unknot, given some
finite representation of a knot. It is open whether this problem admits a polynomial time
algorithm, that is, whether it lies in the complexity class `P`. It is known to lie in
`NP` [HLP99] and in `coNP` [La21].

Following [HLP99], an instance is a polygonal knot in $\mathbb{R}^3$, given by the list of its
vertices in order; the vertices are integer lattice points, and the input length is the number
of bits needed to write them in binary. Such a polygon is an unknot if some homeomorphism of
$\mathbb{R}^3$ carries it onto a round circle. [HLP99] show that this representation is
polynomial time equivalent to the representation of a knot by a knot diagram, with the crossing
number as input size, so the question does not depend on this choice.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [HLP99] Hass, J., Lagarias, J. C., Pippenger, N. _The computational complexity of knot and
  link problems_. Journal of the ACM 46 (1999), 185-211.
  [arXiv:math/9807016](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807016)
- [La21] Lackenby, M. _The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm_.
  Advances in Mathematics 387 (2021). [arXiv:1604.00290](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00290)
-/

open Computability

namespace UnknottingProblem

local notation "ℝ³" => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- The binary encoding of an integer `z` as a bit string. Every binary digit `b` of `|z|`
(least significant digit first, as in `Computability.encodeNat`) is written as the pair
`[true, b]`, and the number is terminated by the pair `[false, s]`, where `s` is the sign
bit `decide (z < 0)`. This encoding is self-delimiting, and its length is linear in the number
of binary digits of `z`. -/
def encodeInt (z : ℤ) : List Bool :=
  (encodeNat z.natAbs).flatMap (fun b => [true, b]) ++ [false, decide (z < 0)]

/-- The encoding of a list of integer lattice points of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ as a bit string: the three
coordinates of each point are written one after another with `encodeInt`. Since `encodeInt` is
self-delimiting, this encoding is injective, and the length of `encodeVertices p` is linear in
the number of bits needed to write the vertices `p` in binary. -/
def encodeVertices (p : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : List Bool :=
  p.flatMap fun v => (List.ofFn v).flatMap encodeInt

/-- The point of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with integer coordinates `v`. -/
def toPoint (v : Fin 3 → ℤ) : ℝ³ := WithLp.toLp 2 fun i => (v i : ℝ)

/-- The closed polygon with vertices `p₀, …, pₙ₋₁` (listed in order): the union of the
closed segments `[pᵢ, pᵢ₊₁]`, with indices taken modulo `n`, so that the last vertex is
joined to the first one. -/
def polygon (p : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Set ℝ³ :=
  ⋃ i : Fin p.length, segment ℝ (toPoint (p.get i)) (toPoint (p.get (finRotate _ i)))

/-- The standard round circle in $\mathbb{R}^3$: the unit circle in the plane $z = 0$. -/
def trivialKnot : Set ℝ³ := {x | x 0 ^ 2 + x 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ x 2 = 0}

/-- A subset `K` of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is an *unknot* (or *trivial knot*) if some homeomorphism of
$\mathbb{R}^3$ maps `K` onto the standard round circle `trivialKnot`.

In particular such a `K` is a knot, i.e. it is homeomorphic to a circle. Two knots are
equivalent if some homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^3$ carries one onto the other; for the unknot
this agrees with equivalence by ambient isotopy, since a reflection of $\mathbb{R}^3$ preserves
`trivialKnot`, and every orientation preserving homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is isotopic
to the identity. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = trivialKnot

open scoped Classical in
/-- The unknotting problem as a decision problem on bit strings: a word `w` is accepted if and
only if `w` encodes (via `encodeVertices`) a list of integer lattice points whose closed
polygon is an unknot. A word that does not encode any list of points, or that encodes a polygon
which is not a knot (e.g. a self-intersecting one), is rejected. -/
noncomputable def unknotRecognition : ComplexityTheory.DecisionProblem :=
  fun w => decide (∃ p, encodeVertices p = w ∧ IsUnknot (polygon p))

/-- The standard round circle is an unknot. -/
@[category API, AMS 57]
theorem isUnknot_trivialKnot : IsUnknot trivialKnot :=
  ⟨Homeomorph.refl _, Set.image_id _⟩

/-- A polygon with no vertices is empty, hence not an unknot. -/
@[category test, AMS 57]
theorem not_isUnknot_polygon_nil : ¬ IsUnknot (polygon []) := by
  rintro ⟨h, hh⟩
  have : (WithLp.toLp 2 ![1, 0, 0] : ℝ³) ∈ trivialKnot := by
    simp [trivialKnot]
  rw [← hh] at this
  simp [polygon] at this

/-- The polygon on three vertices is the triangle with these vertices. -/
@[category test, AMS 57]
theorem polygon_triangle (a b c : Fin 3 → ℤ) :
    polygon [a, b, c] =
      segment ℝ (toPoint a) (toPoint b) ∪ segment ℝ (toPoint b) (toPoint c) ∪
        segment ℝ (toPoint c) (toPoint a) := by
  simp only [polygon, List.length_cons, List.length_nil]
  rw [Set.iUnion_congr (fun i => by rw [finRotate_succ_apply])]
  ext x
  simp only [Set.mem_iUnion, Set.mem_union, Fin.exists_fin_succ, Fin.isValue]
  simp [List.get]
  tauto

@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem encodeInt_zero : encodeInt 0 = [false, false] := by
  decide +kernel

@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem encodeInt_neg_two : encodeInt (-2) = [true, false, true, true, false, true] := by
  decide +kernel

**Unknotting problem**: can unknots be recognized in polynomial time?

That is, is the following decision problem in the complexity class `P` (decidable by a
deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the input length): given a polygonal knot in
$\mathbb{R}^3$ with integer lattice vertices, encoded in binary, is it the unknot?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem : answer(sorry) ↔ unknotRecognition ∈ ComplexityTheory.P := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem

modeling_decisions: Input representation: a knot is given as a polygonal knot in ℝ³ by the list of its integer-lattice vertices in order (HLP99 §1: 'polygonal representation ... integer lattice point vertices ... input length is the number of bits needed to describe its vertices in binary'). HLP99 prove this is polynomial-time equivalent to the knot-diagram representation with crossing number as size, so membership in P is independent of this choice. A knot-diagram encoding was not used because defining combinatorial diagrams/Reidemeister moves faithfully in Lean is far more error-prone.

Bit-string encoding: `encodeInt` writes each binary digit b of |z| (via Mathlib's `Computability.encodeNat`) as the pair [true, b] and terminates with [false, sign]; `encodeVertices` concatenates the three coordinates of each vertex. This is self-delimiting (hence injective) and its length is linear in the binary input length of HLP99. Words that are not codewords are rejected; recognizing codewords is trivially polynomial, so this does not affect membership in P. Injectivity is not proved in the file (only illustrated by tests).

Reuse of `ComplexityTheory.P` from FormalConjectures/Millenium/PvsNP.lean (languages `List Bool → Bool`, poly-time via Mathlib's `Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime`); importing another problem file follows existing Wikipedia files (e.g. ArtinPrimitiveRootsConjecture imports Millenium.RiemannHypothesis).

Unknot definition: `IsUnknot K := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = trivialKnot` where `trivialKnot` is the unit circle in the plane z = 0. This is the classical 'equivalence of knots by an ambient homeomorphism' (identifying a knot with its image set, as HLP99 do). Orientation-preservation is not required, which is harmless for the unknot because the reflection z ↦ -z preserves `trivialKnot`; agreement with the ambient-isotopy definition used by HLP99/Wikipedia uses the standard fact that orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of ℝ³ are isotopic to the identity. Note `IsUnknot K` implies K is homeomorphic to a circle, so non-knots (self-intersecting or degenerate polygons, e.g. fewer than 3 vertices) are rejected, matching HLP99's question 'Is D a knot diagram that represents the trivial knot?'.

The polygon of a vertex list is the union of the closed segments between cyclically consecutive vertices (`finRotate`), so a list with < 3 vertices gives ∅, a point, or a segment, none of which is an unknot; a vertex list that traces the same simple polygon several times has the same image set and is treated as that knot (the knot is identified with its image, as in HLP99).

Category `research open` per the status; Lackenby's announced quasi-polynomial algorithm and the NP/coNP results are recorded in the docstring as background only. AMS tags 57 (knot theory) and 68 (computer science).
